name: Leaders Who Model Use
title: Leaders Who Model Use
answer: Leaders who model AI use make adoption credible. Staff learn from what leaders do, not just what they say. When leaders use AI openly, follow their own rules, and admit uncertainty, AI becomes a normal tool with limits rather than a directive aimed at others.

sections.body: This idea is about leaders demonstrating the AI habits they expect from staff. It solves the credibility gap that appears when leaders ask others to use AI but do not use it themselves. A leader who shares a draft made with AI and explains what needed fixing shows that the tool is ordinary and imperfect. A leader who never touches AI can make staff feel the technology is for other people. Modeling also sets the tone for following the rules the school has set.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, leaders can show how they use AI for everyday work, such as drafting a newsletter, and then describe the corrections they made. They should follow the same habits recommended in this Volume: remove names before using a general tool, check every fact, and keep decisions with people. When leaders follow the rules they set, staff are more likely to take those rules seriously. The supplied text does not give grade bands, so this practice is described for leaders and staff generally rather than for specific year groups. Leaders can also be open about what they do not know and learn alongside staff.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no study, figure, or evidence label for this idea. It rests on practice and observation rather than research. The text states that staff watch what leaders do more closely than what they say, and that modeling builds credibility. It also states that when leaders cut corners, staff notice. No further evidence is provided.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are about credibility and consistency. Leaders who ask staff to use AI but avoid it themselves send a message that AI is for other people. Leaders who cut corners on the recommended habits risk staff taking the rules less seriously. Decisions stay with people, and leaders should keep decisions human. Leaders do not need to be AI experts, but they should be curious, honest about what they do not know, and willing to learn alongside staff. That openness helps staff feel safe to experiment and to share what goes wrong.
